title: Active Monitoring
explain: Active monitoring means the monitor makes its own test traffic and checks the answer: health pings, synthetic transactions, probes from several regions. Passive monitoring only watches what real users already do. I want both, because passive is blind when nobody is using the system and active only covers the paths I thought to probe.
model:
Two ways to learn that something is broken, and each covers the other's blind spot.

| | Active (probe) | Passive (observe) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | Synthetic traffic you generate | Real traffic: error rate, latency percentiles, logs, traces |
| Strength | Signal even at 3 a.m.; tests an end-to-end path | Truth about real users and every path they take |
| Blind spot | Only what you probe; a shallow probe passes while the real flow is broken | Silent when there is no traffic; only reports after users are hurt |

Probe ladder, shallow to deep:

```
ping / TCP connect  ->  GET /healthz  ->  deep check (touches DB)  ->  synthetic transaction
(host alive)            (process answers)  (dependency works)          (login, add to cart, pay)
```

- **Liveness** = is this process wedged? Failure restarts it. **Readiness** = can it take traffic now? Failure removes it from the [load balancer](#/sd/f/load-balancing).
- **Detection time** is about `interval x failure threshold`.
- Probe from several places and alert on a quorum, so one flaky prober cannot page you.
- It is the pull-based sibling of [heartbeats](#/sd/f/heartbeat-lease): there the monitored side pushes.

details.q: At 3 a.m. a deploy breaks checkout, yet error-rate alerts stay quiet. Why, and what closes the gap?
details.a: Nobody tried to check out, so passive metrics saw no errors. A synthetic checkout run on a schedule against a dedicated test account would fail and page. Passive monitoring needs traffic to have something to say.

details.q: Should the liveness probe check the database?
details.a: No. If the database blips for 20 seconds and every pod fails liveness, the orchestrator restarts all of them at once and a brief dependency blip becomes a full outage. Liveness checks only that the process responds; dependency health belongs in readiness, which just stops sending traffic.

details.q: How long until a broken node is declared unhealthy?
details.a: Roughly interval x failure threshold, measured from the last good probe. Probing every 10 s with 3 consecutive failures required means up to about 30 s. Shorter intervals and lower thresholds detect faster but raise false alarms and probe load.

details.q: Your uptime checker runs in one data center and pages a few times a week, always self-resolving. What do you change?
details.a: Probe from three or more locations and alert only when a majority fail for a few consecutive intervals. A single prober cannot tell 'the service is down' from 'my path to the service is down'.

details.q: Is a static 200 OK from /healthz enough?
details.a: It proves only that the process can answer. A deeper check that touches the database proves more but can itself cause an outage if it is expensive or if the dependency flaps. A common compromise is a cheap liveness probe, a dependency-aware readiness probe, and a low-rate synthetic transaction for the real flow.

details.q: What are the costs of probing?
details.a: Probes consume capacity, can create test data (orders, accounts), and can skew metrics. Mark synthetic traffic with a header, use a dedicated test account, clean up after, and exclude it from business dashboards.

details.q: How do active checks tie into failover?
details.a: They are the detector: consecutive failed probes mark a node unhealthy, which triggers removal from rotation or [failover](#/sd/f/failover), and alerts on the [SLIs](#/sd/f/sli-slo-sla) you promised.

prompts.q: Contrast active and passive monitoring and say why production uses both.
points: Active sends its own probes or synthetic transactions on a schedule
Passive observes real traffic: error rate, latency percentiles, logs
Passive is blind with no traffic and only reports after users are hit
Active covers only what you probe and adds load
Combine: passive drives SLO alerting, active catches silent breakage and verifies recovery

prompts.q: Design the health checks for a web service behind a load balancer.
points: Liveness: process responds, failure restarts it
Readiness: dependencies usable, failure removes it from the load balancer only
Keep dependency checks out of liveness to avoid restart storms
Synthetic transaction at low rate against a test account
Multi-region probes, alert on quorum, interval x threshold sets detection time

prompts.q: Explain the 3 a.m. broken-checkout scenario and how you would have caught it.
points: No traffic means no errors for passive metrics
Scheduled synthetic checkout fails and pages
Probe the full end-to-end path, not just the front door
Mark and clean up the test data
